doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

chapter: Life in New York and session work
title: Leaving New York for Florida and the car and gear problem
summary: He left New York for quality of life, and describes parking and hauling a bass in Manhattan.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Sounds good. What prompted you to move to Florida?

I got tired of the New York situation. Life there is, well it’s not a highly habitable place, let’s face it. It’s dingy and dark and dank, and you need lots of stimulants just to get by, feeling like you’re not a caged animal living in this little crystalline structure of boxes that the humans walk from box to box all day. And that just got to me after a while, I just figured there was a better of quality of life somewhere, and my parents already lived in Florida so I sort of did the stepping stone thing there again, stayed with them for about a year.
Did you have a family in New York?

No, I didn’t. I never could have afforded it. I didn’t have a car, I didn’t have a family, and nothing like that. I moved out to Fort Lee, New Jersey to be able to have a car, because I didn’t have to pay for parking out there, I could park on the street out there. But you really have to have a garage in Manhattan. You can’t park on the street, you’re on a schedule just to park, because there’s the alternate side, and it’s free until 7 A.M. and then if you’re not working that day you have to move your car to the other side of the street, it might take you three hours to find a spot. It’s like a job. You’re just better off paying your three, four, these days probably six, seven hundred dollars a month. Another rent, for your car space. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

I’ve often thought when we go to a gig in Utica, we can leave, whatever, 45 minutes before the gig and get there and park in front of the place usually. I’ve often wondered, man, what’s it like to play a gig in Manhattan, if you’ve got gear? You’ve got a bass, and let’s say you’ve got an amp. I mean, how do you do that?

Bless you, Monk. I don’t think anyone else has ever asked me a question like that. It’s inconvenient to say the least, lugging an amp and a bass around. It’ll make you crazy, because I mean I had dreams about my bass getting rained on, or kicked or stolen, or you know, all kinds of things. You become very physically welded to this object, and it’s a severe pain, believe me, it really is, or can be.
